destination.name: The Lowcountry
destination.pitch: Three walkable towns and a string of barrier islands between them, where the food is the best in the American South and the history is either told honestly or sold as a wedding lawn, sometimes on the same road.

because.nature: Salt marsh, boneyard beaches at Botany Bay and Hunting Island, and two barrier islands with no cars and no shops, though none of it is dramatic and almost none of it has a hill.
because.exploration: Six bases in two states on one two hundred mile drive, and the distance between Cannonborough and Hogg Hummock is much bigger than the map suggests.
because.food: Whole hog barbecue, Gullah Geechee kitchens like Bertha's and Gullah Grub, oysters shovelled onto a table at Bowens Island, and shrimp bought off the boat at Darien and Frogmore.
because.relaxation: Edisto has no chain restaurants and no hotel strip, and Beaufort is the one town where you can do nothing without feeling you are wasting a ticket.
because.culture: The International African American Museum, McLeod, Owens-Thomas, Penn Center and Pin Point together tell the story properly, and the Gullah Geechee corridor is a living culture rather than a display.
because.adventure: Tidal creek paddling and a seventeen mile undeveloped beach on Cumberland, but nothing here is hard.
because.city: Charleston and Savannah are small, walkable and genuinely good at night, and neither takes more than three days.

destination.caveat: From June to September the heat sits near 33C with humidity to match and a thunderstorm most afternoons, the sand gnats on the marsh at dawn and dusk are worse than the mosquitoes, and you need a rental car for everything outside the three town centres. Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

cities.name: Charleston
cities.base: Cannonborough Elliottborough or the top of King around Spring Street. You walk to the best restaurants in about six minutes, you are twenty minutes from the Battery on foot, and the rooms are eighty d

cities.name: Sullivan's Island and Mount Pleasant
cities.base: Old Village in Mount Pleasant, near Pitt Street, because Sullivan's Island itself has no hotels at all. You get Shem Creek and the causeway to the beach in ten minutes, and downtown Charleston in fift

cities.name: Edisto Beach
cities.base: A rented house behind the dunes on Palmetto Boulevard, or the Wyndham at the state park end. There is no hotel strip, no chain anything and one small supermarket, which is the reason people come and t

cities.name: Beaufort
cities.base: Downtown between Bay Street and the Point, so you can walk to dinner and to the waterfront park. It is the best value of the three towns and the only one where you will not fight for a parking space.

cities.name: Savannah
cities.base: The squares south of Liberty Street, around Monterey or Chatham, rather than River Street. You are five minutes from Forsyth Park and Jones Street and out of range of the bachelorette parties on Bay.

cities.name: Darien
cities.base: On or near the Darien waterfront by the shrimp docks. It is a shrimping town of about fifteen hundred people with two good restaurants and very little else, and you are here because it is twenty minut

cities.name: The Ashley River plantations and James Island
cities.base: Nowhere to sleep and no reason to try. Four plantation sites strung along Highway 61 plus McLeod on James Island, all of them thirty to forty minutes from downtown Charleston by car, with no bus and n

cities.name: St Helena Island and Hunting Island
cities.base: No hotels on St Helena and only a campground on Hunting Island, so you do this out of Beaufort. Fifteen minutes to Penn Center, thirty five to the lighthouse, one road the whole way.

cities.name: Tybee Island and Fort Pulaski
cities.base: Tybee has rental houses but sleeping out here costs you the Savannah evenings and gains you a twenty minute drive. Treat it as a day: the fort on the way out, the beach and the lighthouse in the middl

cities.name: Sapelo Island
cities.base: There are a handful of rooms in Hogg Hummock and at the Reynolds Mansion, but they must be booked through a resident host who also books your ferry, so for a normal trip this is a half day out of Dari

cities.name: Cumberland Island
cities.base: Camping and the Greyfield Inn are the only beds and both need booking months out, so this is a day boat from St Marys, which is an hour south of Darien. Nine in the morning out, a quarter to five back

outings.name: The Sapelo ferry and the island tour
outings.why: Half past eight from the Meridian dock, four hours on the island by van with a guide, back by half past one. Wednesdays and Saturdays only, fifteen seats, booked by telephone, and if the sound is rough it does not run.
outings.fallback: Fort King George and the Darien shrimp docks, then Hofwyl-Broadfield down the road.

outings.name: The Cumberland day boat: Dungeness, Sea Camp and the River Trail
outings.why: Nine o'clock out of St Marys, forty five minutes across, then about six hours on foot between the ruins, the beach and the forest before the quarter to five boat. No shop, no water beyond the docks, and the sand road is flat but long.
outings.season: Daily March to November, Thursday to Monday December to Febr
outings.fallback: The eleven forty five boat and the quarter to three return, which gives you Dungeness and the beach and nothing else.

outings.name: Ashley River Road: Drayton Hall and Beyond the Fields
outings.why: Drayton Hall on the ten o'clock tour, lunch at Middleton, then Beyond the Fields at two. Two sites in a day is the honest maximum, and Drayton is shut on Tuesdays.
outings.fallback: McLeod Plantation on James Island, ten minutes from downtown, which does the same history in two hours.

outings.name: Botany Bay at low tide
outings.why: The causeway and the boneyard beach, timed to a falling tide or the trees are standing in water. Free, closed every Tuesday, and there is a mile of walking in full sun with no shade at the beach end.
outings.fallback: Edisto Beach State Park boardwalk and the shell midden trail, which works at any tide.

outings.name: Penn Center and Gullah Grub on St Helena
outings.why: The York W. Bailey Museum on the ten o'clock tour, Darrah Hall and Brick Baptist on foot, the Chapel of Ease ruins, then lunch at Gullah Grub. Tuesday to Saturday only, because Penn Center shuts Sunday and Monday.
outings.fallback: The Old Sheldon Church ruins and the Beaufort National Cemetery, which are both free and open every day.

outings.name: The Hunting Island lighthouse and the boneyard
outings.why: Eight dollars into the park, the 167 step climb if the tower is open that day, the north end boneyard beach at low tide, and the marsh boardwalk at the end of the afternoon. Tide table decides the whole shape of it.
outings.season: Year round, best October to May
outings.fallback: The marsh boardwalk and the nature centre alone, which take an hour and work at high tide.

outings.name: Bonaventure at eight, then Pin Point and Wormsloe
outings.why: The cemetery before the coaches, the Pin Point oyster factory museum at ten, Wormsloe's oak avenue after lunch. Pin Point is only open a few days a week and it is the part worth building the day around.
outings.season: Year round, Thursday to Saturday for Pin Point
outings.fallback: Bonaventure and Wormsloe only, then the Forsyth Park market if it is a Saturday.

outings.name: An oyster roast at Bowens Island
outings.why: Steamed cluster oysters shovelled onto a table over the marsh at sunset, twenty minutes from downtown. Closed Sundays and Mondays, the queue starts before they open, and local oysters are properly in season in the cold months.
outings.season: Best October to April for local clusters
outings.fallback: The Ordinary on upper King for the raw bar, or The Wreck across the harbour in Mount Pleasant.

outings.name: The Fort Sumter boat from Liberty Square
outings.why: Two and a quarter hours door to door with an hour on the fort, and the harbour crossing past Castle Pinckney is the better part. The half past nine sailing beats the heat and the crowd.
outings.fallback: Fort Moultrie on Sullivan's Island, which you drive to, costs ten dollars and is a better fort.

outings.name: The Edisto tidal creeks by kayak
outings.why: Three hours on a rising tide through spartina with dolphins and wood storks, flat water and no skill needed. It has to be morning because the afternoon storm is close to daily from June to September.
outings.fallback: The Edisto Beach State Park maritime forest trail and the shell midden, ninety minutes on foot.

outings.name: Tybee: the fort, the light and the back river
outings.why: Fort Pulaski at nine on the way out, the Cockspur marsh trail, the lighthouse climb, the beach through the hot part, then the back river for sunset. The lighthouse is shut on Tuesdays and the whole island parks by meter.
outings.fallback: Fort Pulaski and the Cockspur trail alone, which is a three hour morning.

places.name: International African American Museum
places.note: Built on Gadsden's Wharf, where close to half of all enslaved Africans brought to North America first stood on land, and the building is deliberately lifted off that ground on pillars.

places.name: Old Slave Mart Museum
places.note: The only surviving building in the country used as a slave auction gallery, two small rooms that do more damage in an hour than any plantation tour.

places.name: Aiken-Rhett House Museum
places.note: Preserved rather than restored, so you walk through the intact work yard, kitchen block and slave quarters with the plaster still falling, which is the honest version of a Charleston single house.

places.name: The High Battery and White Point Garden
places.note: Half an hour on the seawall with the harbour on one side and the money on the other, best an hour before sunset when the heat lets go.

places.name: Mother Emanuel AME Church
places.note: Founded by Denmark Vesey's congregation, burned by the city in 1822, and the site of the 2015 murders, so go quietly and do not treat the sidewalk memorial as a photo stop.

places.name: Charleston City Market
places.note: Four blocks of sunglasses, hot sauce and pralines, and the only reason to walk it is the sweetgrass basket sewers at the Meeting Street end, who are the real thing and price accordingly. Buy a basket, skip the rest.

places.name: The Fort Sumter boat from Liberty Square
places.note: Two and a quarter hours door to door with about an hour on the fort itself, and the harbour crossing is the better half of it.

places.name: Hannibal's Kitchen
places.note: Crab rice, shark steak and a shrimp and grits breakfast served from before eight, family run since 1985, cash friendly and no atmosphere to speak of. Closed Sundays and the weekday hours have contracted, so call first.

places.name: Bertha's Kitchen
places.note: A steam table in a cinderblock room, lima beans and okra soup and fried whiting, a James Beard America's Classics winner run by the same family. Weekday lunch only and the line is at its worst at noon.

places.name: Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ
places.note: Whole hog cooked over coals the way Scott learned it in Hemingway, South Carolina, with vinegar and pepper sauce and no sweetness, and the pork skins are the point.

places.name: Chubby Fish
places.note: Whatever came off the boat that morning, written on a board, no reservations at all, so put a name down when the door opens at five or eat at the bar late.

places.name: The Ordinary
places.note: A bank hall turned oyster house with a cold shellfish tower that is worth the money and a dining room loud enough that you will not hear each other. Closed Tuesdays, service starts at four.

places.name: Fort Moultrie
places.note: Free-standing brick forts from 1776 to 1947 on one site, and the newer exhibit finally deals with the quarantine pest houses on this island where tens of thousands of captive Africans were held before sale.

places.name: The Station 22 beach path
places.note: Sand dunes, a wide flat beach and no commercial strip at all, which also means no rentals, no toilets and strictly enforced residential parking.

places.name: The Obstinate Daughter
places.note: Wood-fired pizza, Geechie Boy grits and good pasta upstairs over the dunes, and it books out a week ahead in summer.

places.name: Poe's Tavern
places.note: Burgers and cold beer in a low dark room named for the private who was stationed at Moultrie, and it is the island's default lunch after the beach.

places.name: Home Team BBQ Sullivan's Island
places.note: Smoked wings, a decent pulled pork sandwich and a frozen drink called the Game Changer that has ended more afternoons than the heat has.

places.name: The Shem Creek boardwalk
places.note: A boardwalk over spartina marsh with the working shrimp fleet tied up on the far bank and dolphins in the channel at a falling tide.

places.name: The Wreck of the Richard and Charlene
places.note: A screened tin shed on the creek behind a shrimp dock, fried seafood and boiled shrimp on paper plates, dinner only and closed Sundays.

places.name: The sweetgrass basket stands on Highway 17
places.note: Roadside plywood stands where Mount Pleasant women sew coiled sweetgrass baskets, a craft carried directly from Sierra Leone and Senegal, and a small one honestly costs eighty dollars because it took two days.

places.name: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site
places.note: Twenty-eight acres left of Snee Farm with a free exhibit that spends most of its space on the enslaved people who worked it rather than on the Constitution signer who owned them.

places.name: Boone Hall Plantation
places.note: The nine brick slave cabins and the live Gullah presentation by descendants are real and worth an hour. Everything around them is a wedding lawn, a strawberry festival and a haunted trail, and the famous oak avenue is sold as a backdrop, so if you have one plantation day give it to McLeod or to Midd

places.name: Botany Bay Plantation Heritage Preserve
places.note: A causeway walk out to a boneyard beach of dead oaks and palmettos standing in the surf, free, and shut every Tuesday for management. Take nothing off the beach, not one shell, the rule is enforced.

places.name: Edisto Beach State Park
places.note: Four miles of quiet beach plus a maritime forest trail to a shell midden, and the eight dollar day fee is the whole cost.

places.name: Edisto Island Serpentarium
places.note: Two brothers who caught snakes on this island their whole lives, outdoor gardens rather than tanks, and it only opens in the warm months so check the season before driving out.

places.name: Pressley's at the Marina
places.note: Fried and broiled local shrimp over the creek at Big Bay, the sunset seats go first, and the kitchen slows badly on a full Saturday.

places.name: SeaCow Eatery
places.note: The island's breakfast, shrimp and grits and pancakes, full by half past eight on a Saturday in July.

places.name: Whaley's
places.note: An old filling station turned beach bar, no view, no menu to speak of, and the only place on the island where you will end up talking to residents.

places.name: Flowers Seafood Company
places.note: Shrimp off the boats at the marina, sold by the pound, which is the cheapest good dinner on the island if your rental has a pot.

places.name: McConkey's Jungle Shack
places.note: Fish tacos, burgers and a crab cake sandwich in a screened shack, and the hours shrink hard outside summer.

places.name: The Edisto tidal creeks by kayak
places.note: Three hours through spartina on a rising tide with dolphins and wood storks, and you go early because the afternoon thunderstorm is close to a daily event from June to August.

places.name: Edisto Island Museum
places.note: One room run by the island's historic preservation society, strongest on the Gullah community and the freedmen's settlements rather than on the planters. Opening hours are short and seasonal, so call the same morning.

places.name: Henry C. Chambers Waterfront Park
places.note: Swings facing the Beaufort River, shrimp boats going up the reach, and the whole of downtown is behind you in two blocks.

places.name: The Point
places.neighborhood: The Point, east of Carteret Street
places.note: Antebellum houses under live oaks on a grid of quiet residential streets, which the Union army occupied in November 1861 and which is why they are all still standing.

places.name: Beaufort National Cemetery
places.note: Laid out by Lincoln in 1863, and the graves of the 55th Massachusetts and the Union dead from Folly Island are the reason to walk in.

places.name: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park visitor centre
places.note: The newest unit in the park system and the only one telling the Reconstruction story, small, free, and the ranger talk is better than the exhibit. Hours are limited and change, so call ahead.

places.name: John Mark Verdier House Museum
places.note: A 1804 merchant's house on Bay Street, useful mostly for how plainly it explains where Sea Island cotton money came from.

places.name: Pat Conroy Literary Center
places.note: Donation only, run by people who knew him, and it will make you want to reread The Water Is Wide before you drive to Daufuskie.

places.name: Old Sheldon Church Ruins
places.note: Brick colonnade and no roof under old oaks, twenty five minutes north of town, free, and busy with photographers by mid morning.

places.name: The Sands and the Port Royal boat landing
places.note: A shell beach on Battery Creek with an observation tower over the marsh, where Beaufort goes and visitors mostly do not.

places.name: Saltus River Grill
places.note: The good dinner in Beaufort, raw bar and local fish on the water, dinner seven nights from five, and you want a reservation on a weekend.

places.name: Q on Bay
places.note: Lowcountry barbecue buffet with hash and rice, which is the South Carolina plate you will not get anywhere else, and the days it opens shift so check.

places.name: Old Bull Tavern
places.note: A dark narrow room with a real wine list and a small kitchen, and it is the only place downtown with any life after ten.

places.name: Lowcountry Produce Market and Cafe
places.note: Breakfast and a jar of their pickled okra to take home, in the old post office, and it shuts by mid afternoon.

places.name: Owens-Thomas House and Slave Quarters
places.note: The single best history hour in Savannah since the 2018 reinterpretation, because the tour now starts in the intact urban slave quarters with the original haint blue ceiling and works upward. One ticket covers all three Telfair sites for seven days.

places.name: First African Baptist Church
places.note: Congregation organised in 1773, the building raised by enslaved people working at night, and the air holes drilled in the floor for people hidden underneath are still there. Tours run on a fixed timetable, so ring the office.

places.name: Bonaventure Cemetery
places.note: A hundred acres of Spanish moss, azaleas and Victorian statuary on a bluff over the Wilmington River, free, and much better at eight in the morning than in the tour bus hours.

places.name: Laurel Grove South Cemetery
places.note: The burial ground for Savannah's free and enslaved Black residents, where Andrew Bryan and the founders of the Black churches lie, underfunded and almost empty of visitors.

places.name: Forsyth Park and the Saturday market
places.note: Thirty acres of oaks and the city's farmers market at the south end on Saturday mornings, which is where the Sapelo Island red peas and the boiled peanuts are.

places.name: Wormsloe State Historic Site
places.note: A mile and a half of live oaks over the drive, then tabby ruins at the end of it. The oak avenue is what the photographs sell and the tabby was laid by enslaved labour the site has only recently started naming properly.

places.name: Pin Point Heritage Museum
places.note: The old A. S. Varn oyster and crab factory, told by the Gullah Geechee community that worked it from 1926 to 1985 and still lives on the bluff. Open only a few days a week and the hours are short, so confirm before driving out.

places.name: Mrs Wilkes Dining Room
places.note: Communal tables, fried chicken and eleven sides put down at once, thirty five dollars a head, cash or cheque only, weekday lunch and nothing else. Get in the line on Jones Street by half past ten.

places.name: The Grey
places.note: Mashama Bailey cooking port city food in a 1938 Greyhound terminal that was segregated when it was built, and the fact of where you are sitting is part of the meal. Closed Mondays, book on Resy weeks out.

places.name: Common Thread
places.note: A Victorian house south of the squares doing the best cooking in town that is not on a tourist itinerary, seven nights from five.

places.name: Narobia's Grits and Gravy
places.note: Salmon patties, shrimp and gravy over grits, fourteen dollars, and it is a breakfast counter that stops serving in the early afternoon. Days off move around, so call.

places.name: The horse-drawn carriage tours off Bay Street
places.note: Thirty five dollars for a scripted loop of the squares that skips slavery almost entirely, and the horses stand in the heat. Walk the squares yourself with the Owens-Thomas tour in your head instead.

places.name: Fort King George
places.note: A reconstructed 1721 cypress blockhouse over the Altamaha marsh, plus the remains of the sawmills and the tabby, and almost nobody is there.

places.name: The Darien shrimp docks
places.note: One of the last working shrimp fleets on the Georgia coast tied up under the US-17 bridge, and late afternoon is when the boats come in.

places.name: Skipper's Fish Camp
places.note: Wild Georgia shrimp from the boats twenty yards away, an oyster bar, and a deck over the river that is the only dinner view in town.

places.name: B and J's Steaks and Seafood
places.note: A roadside room with no view where the shrimp is the same boat and the bill is fifteen dollars lower, which is the local answer.

places.name: Butler Island
places.note: A brick rice mill chimney and the old dikes in the Altamaha delta, on the estate whose people were sold in Savannah in 1859 in the largest slave auction in American history. There is almost no interpretation on site, which is its own statement.

places.name: Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation
places.note: A rice plantation that stayed in one family until 1973, with hourly guided tours that do name the enslaved workers who built and ran the dikes rather than skipping to the dairy years.

places.name: Harris Neck National Wildlife Refuge
places.note: Wood storks and painted buntings on old airfield loops, and the land was taken in 1942 from a Gullah Geechee community that has been trying to get it back ever since.

places.name: The Sapelo Island Visitors Centre at Meridian
places.note: Where you check in for the ferry and the island tour, fifteen minutes before departure, and the exhibit is a decent twenty minutes if you are early.

places.name: The Altamaha delta by kayak
places.note: Old rice canals and cypress into the biggest undammed river delta on the east coast, flat water, and the heat and the sand gnats decide how long you last.

places.name: McLeod Plantation Historic Site
places.note: The one to do if you do only one. The guided tour is told from the row of cabins where freed people were still living in 1990, the big house is almost an afterthought, and nobody gets married here.

places.name: Drayton Hall
places.note: Unfurnished, unrestored, no electricity, a 1740s house left exactly as it survived, with an African American cemetery kept unmown at the descendants' request. Closed Tuesdays and the front gate shuts at three.

places.name: Middleton Place
places.note: The oldest landscaped garden in the country, dug by enslaved people over ten years, and the site says so on the signage now. House museum is fifteen dollars more and skippable.

places.name: Beyond the Fields at Middleton Place
places.note: Forty minutes, included with admission, run at eleven, twelve, two and three, and it is the reason to come here rather than the camellias.

places.name: Magnolia Plantation and Gardens
places.note: Sells itself on azaleas, a petting zoo and a swamp boardwalk, and the base ticket will let you spend a whole day here without learning anything about the people who dug it. Only worth it if you add the cabin tour below.

places.name: From Slavery to Freedom at Magnolia
places.note: Five restored cabins on the old street, told through named families who stayed into the 1990s, and it is a genuinely good forty five minutes bolted onto a garden attraction.

places.name: Angel Oak
places.note: A live oak somewhere between four and five hundred years old with limbs resting on the ground, free, ten minutes and a photograph, and the car park fills by ten.

places.name: Bowens Island Restaurant
places.note: Steamed oysters shovelled onto a table with a hole cut in it, a cinderblock room over the marsh, and you shuck your own. Closed Sundays and Mondays and the cluster oysters are seasonal.

places.name: The Middleton Place Restaurant
places.note: Hoppin' John, okra soup and Carolina Gold rice cooked properly, and it is the only decent lunch on the plantation road.

places.name: Folly Beach County Park
places.note: The west end of Folly where the river meets the sea, lifeguards and toilets, twenty dollars to park, and far calmer than the pier end.

places.name: Penn Center and the York W. Bailey Museum
places.neighborhood: St Helena Island, Penn Center Circle
places.note: One of the first schools in the South for people freed from slavery, opened in 1862, later where King and the SCLC planned campaigns, and still the centre of Gullah cultural life. Museum is Tuesday to Saturday with guided tours at ten, twelve and three.

places.name: Brick Baptist Church
places.neighborhood: St Helena Island, Martin Luther King Jr Drive
places.note: Built in 1855 by enslaved people who had to sit in the gallery, handed to the Black congregation in 1861, and the Penn School's first classrooms were in it.

places.name: Darrah Hall
places.note: The oldest building on the Penn campus and now a National Park Service unit, free, with rangers who will talk for as long as you want.

places.name: The Chapel of Ease ruins
places.neighborhood: St Helena Island, Lands End Road
places.note: Tabby walls of a 1740s chapel burned in 1886, free, five minutes off the main road, and roofless under the oaks.

places.name: Lands End Road
places.note: A tunnel of live oak and moss down to a small landing at the end of the island, and it is a drive and a short walk rather than a hike.

places.name: Gullah Grub
places.neighborhood: St Helena Island, Sea Island Parkway
places.note: Bill Green's kitchen, shrimp gravy, red rice and okra soup cooked the way it is cooked in the houses around it, which is the whole reason to drive out here. Hours and days move, so telephone the morning of.

places.name: Gay Fish Company
places.note: A family shrimp dock since 1948 selling off the boat, and the boats in the photographs from Forrest Gump were theirs.

places.name: The Hunting Island lighthouse
places.note: The only lighthouse in South Carolina you can climb, 167 steps, inside an eight dollar state park. The tower is not open every day, so ring the park office before you build a morning on it.

places.name: The Hunting Island boneyard beach
places.note: Storm-killed pines and palmettos lying in the surf on an eroding shoreline, walkable at low tide and pointless at high, so check the tide table first.

places.name: The Hunting Island marsh boardwalk
places.note: A long boardwalk out over open salt marsh to a viewing platform, flat, ten minutes each way, and the best light is the last hour.

places.name: Fort Pulaski National Monument
places.note: The brick fort that rifled Union artillery holed in thirty hours in 1862 and ended masonry forts everywhere, with the shot damage left unrepaired, and it is where the first enslaved people in Georgia were freed.

places.name: The Cockspur Island lighthouse trail
places.note: A flat mile through marsh to a view of the small lighthouse standing in the river, free with the fort ticket, and it floods on a spring high tide.

places.name: Tybee Island Light Station and Museum
places.note: 178 steps, a working first order lens, and the ticket includes the gun battery museum opposite. Closed every Tuesday.

places.name: Tybee North Beach
places.note: Wide sand under the lighthouse with container ships passing close enough to read, quieter than the pier end, and parking is paid and strictly ticketed.

places.name: The Tybee pier and pavilion
places.note: T-shirt shops, a fishing pier and the loudest stretch of the island, fine for an hour after the beach and not much more.

places.name: The Crab Shack
places.note: Low country boil on a creek deck with an alligator pen and a gift shop, entirely a tourist operation, and still a decent pile of shrimp at sunset if you accept what it is.

places.name: AJ's Dockside
places.note: The back river sunset from a deck the locals actually use, and you put your name down and wait with a drink because they will not hold a table.

places.name: Sundae Cafe
places.note: In a strip mall next to a supermarket, and it is the best cooking on the island by a distance, so book.

places.name: Tybee Island Marine Science Center
places.note: Small, aimed at children, but the beach walks and the sea turtle work are run by people who know the island's ecology better than anyone.

places.name: Kayaking to Little Tybee
places.note: An undeveloped barrier island bigger than Tybee itself, reachable only by boat, and the crossing needs the tide with you in both directions so go with a guide.

places.name: The state ferry from Meridian
places.note: Twenty to thirty minutes across Doboy Sound on the Georgia DNR boat, and there is no other public way on or off the island, so missing the return is a real problem.

places.name: The Sapelo Island public tour
places.note: Four hours including the ferry, by van, Wednesdays at half past eight and Saturdays at nine, fifteen people maximum and you book it by telephone with the visitors centre. This is the only way to see the island without a resident host.

places.name: Hogg Hummock
places.note: About forty residents left of a Saltwater Geechee community descended from the people enslaved on Thomas Spalding's plantation, and McIntosh County's 2023 rezoning to allow bigger houses is an active fight over whether it survives.

places.name: The Reynolds Mansion
places.note: The tobacco heir's pink South End house with a circus-themed basement bar, included on some tour dates and not others.

places.name: Sapelo Island Lighthouse
places.note: Red and white striped, 1820, restored and standing at the mouth of Doboy Sound, and the tour usually stops here for fifteen minutes.

places.name: Nanny Goat Beach
places.note: Undeveloped sand and dune with a research boardwalk, no facilities, no shade and no shop anywhere on the island, so carry your own water.

places.name: Behavior Cemetery
places.note: An active Geechee burial ground still in use, held in common by the community, and you go only if the tour takes you and you keep your camera down.

places.name: First African Baptist Church at Raccoon Bluff
places.note: Built in 1900 by the freedmen's community that bought this end of the island, abandoned when the residents were moved to Hogg Hammock, and restored by their descendants.

places.name: The Sapelo shell rings
places.note: Four thousand year old rings of oyster shell, among the oldest built structures in North America, and they look like low wooded banks until someone explains them.

places.name: The Cumberland Island ferry from St Marys
places.note: Forty five minutes each way, departures at nine and a quarter to twelve, returns at a quarter past ten, a quarter to three and a quarter to five, and you must buy both legs. Book weeks ahead in spring.

places.name: Cumberland Island National Seashore entry
places.note: Fifteen dollars a head on top of the ferry, card only since the island went cashless, and there is no shop, no food and no drinking water beyond the two docks.

places.name: The Dungeness ruins
places.note: The burned shell of the Carnegie mansion with horses grazing in the old lawns, about a mile from the Sea Camp dock on flat sand road.

places.name: Sea Camp beach
places.note: Seventeen miles of undeveloped Atlantic beach reached through a live oak tunnel, no lifeguards, no shade and no way to buy anything.

places.name: The Ice House Museum
places.note: One free room by the dock covering the Timucua, the Carnegies and the Black community at the north end, and it is the only interpretation on the island.

places.name: The River Trail
places.note: Three and a half miles of flat maritime forest along the sound between the two docks, shaded, and the way to link the ruins and the beach on a day ticket.

places.name: The feral horses on the dunes
places.note: Around two hundred unmanaged horses, thin and tick-bitten and not a conservation success story, and the Park Service asks for fifty feet of distance because they kick.

places.name: Plum Orchard
places.note: A Carnegie Georgian Revival house eight miles north of Sea Camp, reachable on foot or on the paid island tour and not on a normal day ticket.

places.name: First African Baptist Church at the Settlement
places.note: A one room whitewashed church built in 1893 by the freedmen's settlement at the north end, seventeen miles from the dock, so it needs the all-day Lands and Legacies tour rather than a walk.
